uncited: It builds on the [GPU Ray Casting Pipeline](14281-gpu-ray-casting-pipeline.md) by offloading the ray traversal and compositing steps to the graphics hardware.
*   Transfer functions (mapping scalar values to color and opacity).
*   Camera parameters (position, orientation, projection).
*   Pre-computed gradient data (optional, see optimization).
*   Final image (color and alpha per pixel).
*   **Volume Texture:** 3D texture storing scalar values.
*   **Gradient Texture:** 3D RGBA texture storing pre-computed gradients.
**Ray-Volume Intersection:** Determine the entry and exit points of the ray with the volume bounding box.
**Step Size Calculation:** Determine the step size along the ray.
This may be fixed or adaptive based on resolution and desired accuracy.
Sample the volume texture at the current ray position to get the scalar value $v$.
Sample the transfer function using $v$ to get color $c$ and opacity $\alpha$.
If pre-computed gradients are used, sample the gradient texture at the current position to get $\nabla v$.
Advance the ray position by the step size.
If $A_{acc} \geq 1$ or the ray has exited the volume, terminate the loop.
**Post-Processing:** Apply any final image processing (e.g., tone mapping, anti-aliasing).
*   **Step Size:** Determines sampling density.
Smaller steps increase accuracy but reduce performance.
*   **Gradient Pre-computation:** Trade-off between memory usage and computational cost.
*   **Boundary Conditions:** Ensure correct handling of rays that do not intersect the volume or intersect only at the boundary.
*   **Time Complexity:** $O(N \cdot M)$, where $N$ is the number of pixels and $M$ is the average number of samples per ray.
Performance degrades with large step sizes or complex transfer functions.
*   **When Not to Use:** When high spatial resolution is critical and performance is not a constraint, or when memory bandwidth is severely limited.
It was originally developed to overcome the performance limitations of CPU-based raycasting.
